newsitem.title: COMOROS: Fifty confirmed dead in crash of hijacked plane.
newsitem.headline: Fifty confirmed dead in crash of hijacked plane.

text.p: A hijacked Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 767 with 175 passengers and crew aboard crashed into the sea near the Comoro Islands on Saturday, killing at least 50 people.
Airline officials said 30 people survived. Unfavourable weather hampered rescue efforts, the officials said.

They said the pilot and one crew member were among those who survived when the plane, hijacked between Addis Ababa and its first scheduled stop in the Kenyan capital Nairobi, ran out of fuel and ditched while trying to land at Moroni airport.

Thirty bodies of crash victims, mostly Asians and Africans, were laid out under blankets in the conference room of a beach hotel near where the plane came down about 40 km (25 miles) north of Moroni, capital of the Indian Ocean archipelago.
Israel Radio quoted a presidential spokesman in the Comoros as appealing for doctors to go to the scene.

Airline officials said the hijackers were believed to be transit passengers from Bombay. They said the identity of the hijackers was not confirmed but that they may have wanted to hijack the plane to Australia.
Speaking earlier to the BBC World Service, Frederick Chretien, manager of the Galawa beach hotel, said a survivor spoke of seeing two hijackers on board.
"Apparently there are two bombs still in the aircraft and we are waiting for the French forces to investigate," he said.
Airline officials said the plane was carrying 163 passengers and 12 crew members.
The plane, flight ET 961, was hijacked on Saturday morning soon after it took off from Addis Ababa to Abidjan via Nairobi, Brazzaville and Lagos.
Witnesses earlier said the plane broke in two when it plunged into the sea only metres (yards) from shore next to the beach hotel.
Airline officials said the fuselage was seen floating in the sea while the rear part had submerged.
"The plane crashed at around 3:20 local time (1220 GMT)," Chakira Maamoune, a Moroni airport official, told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"I can confirm that the airplane was not in contact with Moroni air traffic control," he said.
Airline officials in the Tanzanian capital Dar es Salaam said they made contact with the plane at about 3 p.m. (1200 GMT).
"The control tower had some contact with the plane but only for five minutes, then it was cut. At that point the plane was around the coastal area of Dar es Salaam," the official said.
After the hijackers took control, it entered Tanzanian airspace and flew east across the Indian Ocean heading for the Comoro Islands.
Ethiopian Airlines is the only airline that crosses the breadth of Africa and has had one of the best safety records among African carriers.
